items.title: Harnesses, Part Three: How Agents Run Forever
items.summary: What happens when an agent outlives its context window — and how it decides what history survives. Read the article for free, here . Created using matplotlib, more on this later. Thanks claude.ai. Alpinists don’t carry the expedition. They cache it. A long climb is staged into camps each stocked with what the next leg needs. Whatever isn’t required stays behind, retrievable if you have to come back, but not dragged any higher. The load that reaches the summit is whatever survived every camp’s decision about what to leave behind. A context window works the same way. Capacity is fixed, the route isn’t, and eventually something has to be left behind. Part Two argued for the rule underneath all of this, never invalidate the cac. Keep the stable part warm and push change to the tail. But Part Two treated a session like a still photograph. It didn’t account for time . Every session ages. The conversation grows. Eventually the window fills and you have to fold. The mechanical outcome is simple a smaller window. The cost is less simple, folding requires an invalidation event. You pay that cost once, rewrite what survives, and continue. But the invalidation isn’t the interesting part. The interesting part is what survives the fold. A good compaction doesn’t merely remove tokens. It compresses a history into something the agent can continue from. And long-running sessions don’t fold once. They fold, work, fold again, and eventually fold the previous fold. The real question is therefore not when should we compact? It’s, what survives a fold of a fold of a fold , and eventually, what disappears? This changes how we should think about compaction. The schedule matters because invalidation costs money. But the compression matters because it determines whether the session is still the same session afterward. And compaction should be the last rung you reach for, not the first. The tail is the bill A request has two economic regions: the prefix that survives, and the tail that grows. The prefix is the system prompt, tool definitions, repo-stable context, rules files. Written once, cached, read back at a fraction of cost on every later turn. It doesn’t grow. It’s the thing we were protecting in Part Two. The tail is everything after. The conversation, tool calls, tool results, thinking blocks, diffs. It grows monotonically. But growth isn’t the tail’s expensive property. Rent is. Every time you type a message and hit enter, the harness doesn’t send the new text alone. It resends the matched prefix, reads it back at the cached rate, and writes whatever’s new at the write premium. The tail rides along on every one of those reads. A hundred and fifty thousand tokens of tail isn’t a static liability sitting in the window. It’s a bill that comes due on every turn, whether the model needs any of it to answer your next question or not. You’re paying rent on your own history every time you press enter, for as long as the session lives. Created with matplotlib. Most of that yellow space turns a 200k context window into 7.5k to ~15k, depending on the harness and many factors. The cache has another clock. Its TTL is refreshed by activity, so idle time can turn the next turn into a cold write. Human think time is a non-advertised cache expense. Compaction is therefore an operation on the tail that is also an operation on the cache. You’re choosing to pay an invalidation cost today to stop paying rent tomorrow. That’s the trade. And before paying it, there are cheaper places to intervene. The ladder There are five moves against tail growth. They aren’t alternatives so much as rungs. The higher you climb, the more existing history you are willing to disturb. One: don’t generate it . Cap the output at the tool. Anthropic’s text editor tool supports max_characters , web search supports max_uses. Codex caps individual tool outputs betwen 10,000 — 16,000 tokens by default, before they reach the compaction calculation. The more disciplined version is snipping . Keep a head and a tail, trim the middle, on the assumption that what a command started with and where it ended matter more than the scroll back between them. The weakness is that you’re truncating before you know what mattered. A stack trace with the relevant frame removed is worse than no stack trace. Two, spill it. Don’t carry the whole observation if you don’t need the whole observation. When a tool result crosses a size threshold, the harness can write it to disk and leave a reference behind. The full artifact survives, the live context doesn’t. This is different from truncation. Nothing was thrown away. A 500k-line build log or terminal result can live on disk while the context contains only its path, metadata, or a searchable index. When the agent needs something from it later, a native search or read tool pulls back only the relevant slice. Keep the artifact. Remove the observation. This is one of the cleanest ways to separate storage from context. The information remains durable without collecting rent on every subsequent turn. The catch is that the harness needs the tools to find it again. Spill-to-disk only works if the agent can search, read, and reason about what it stored. Otherwise you’ve traded context overflow for a filesystem full of things that can’t be retrieve. The convergence here is striking. Several harnesses land on nearly the same threshold. Claude Code spills any tool result over roughly a 100k to disk and hands back a preview plus a path. Hermes uses the same 100k per-result cap. And both make the same pointed exception, the read tool is exempt from spilling , because a spilled read is a path that the agent would only read again. Literally, a read to spill to read, forever. I honestly have gone into infinite loops here. Be careful. The one tool whose whole job is to pull content back is the one tool you must never spill. Three, don’t admit it. Delegate the work. A subagent with the harnesses native tools can read the files, scan the logs, explore the repository, and accumulate a large working context without any of that history entering the parent’s tail. When the task ends, the child’s window disappears and only its return value crosses the boundary. This is genuinely one of the most popular features harnesses shipped this year. However, exploration is not as dangerous as modification. A worker that reads the wrong files costs you a re-run. A worker that edits the wrong files leaves damage behind after its context is gone. Be careful about which model you allow to do a modification. Back in the day, a scout wasn’t typically a high-ranked officer of your kingdom. You sent someone fast and expendable to go look. Looking is cheap and the report is easy to check. An emperor looking to overtake would always send their best to do the taking, the act itself is the thing that can’t be undone. Delegate the scouting to a cheap, disposable context. Reserve your strongest for the move that actually changes the world. And, keep the parent in the loop to verify it. The parent pays for the answer, not the investigation. Four, replace it with a pointer. If the content already exists durably — a file, artifact, generated report, or spilled tool result — the pointer is all the conversation needs. A re-read goes back to where the content lives without carrying the content permanently in the conversation. Anthropic’s memory tool is exactly this, built for you. OpenAI provides similar behavior with their Tools API (Function Calling ). Turn expensive conversational state into a cheap reference to durable state. The catch is that the pointer only saves money while the underlying content stays out of the window. Re-read it and it becomes tail content again, renting from the moment it lands. What happens when an agent outlives its context window — and how it decides what history survives.
Read the article for free, here.
Created using matplotlib, more on this later. Thanks claude.ai.

Alpinists don’t carry the expedition. They cache it.

A long climb is staged into camps each stocked with what the next leg needs. Whatever isn’t required stays behind, retrievable if you have to come back, but not dragged any higher. The load that reaches the summit is whatever survived every camp’s decision about what to leave behind.

A context window works the same way. Capacity is fixed, the route isn’t, and eventually something has to be left behind.

Part Two argued for the rule underneath all of this, never invalidate the cac. Keep the stable part warm and push change to the tail. But Part Two treated a session like a still photograph. It didn’t account for time.

Every session ages. The conversation grows. Eventually the window fills and you have to fold.

The mechanical outcome is simple a smaller window. The cost is less simple, folding requires an invalidation event. You pay that cost once, rewrite what survives, and continue.

But the invalidation isn’t the interesting part.

The interesting part is what survives the fold.

A good compaction doesn’t merely remove tokens. It compresses a history into something the agent can continue from. And long-running sessions don’t fold once. They fold, work, fold again, and eventually fold the previous fold.

The real question is therefore not when should we compact?

It’s, what survives a fold of a fold of a fold, and eventually, what disappears?

This changes how we should think about compaction. The schedule matters because invalidation costs money. But the compression matters because it determines whether the session is still the same session afterward.

And compaction should be the last rung you reach for, not the first.

The tail is the bill

A request has two economic regions: the prefix that survives, and the tail that grows.

The prefix is the system prompt, tool definitions, repo-stable context, rules files. Written once, cached, read back at a fraction of cost on every later turn. It doesn’t grow. It’s the thing we were protecting in Part Two.

The tail is everything after. The conversation, tool calls, tool results, thinking blocks, diffs. It grows monotonically.

But growth isn’t the tail’s expensive property. Rent is.

Every time you type a message and hit enter, the harness doesn’t send the new text alone. It resends the matched prefix, reads it back at the cached rate, and writes whatever’s new at the write premium. The tail rides along on every one of those reads.

A hundred and fifty thousand tokens of tail isn’t a static liability sitting in the window. It’s a bill that comes due on every turn, whether the model needs any of it to answer your next question or not.

You’re paying rent on your own history every time you press enter, for as long as the session lives.

Created with matplotlib. Most of that yellow space turns a 200k context window into 7.5k to ~15k, depending on the harness and many factors.

The cache has another clock. Its TTL is refreshed by activity, so idle time can turn the next turn into a cold write.

Human think time is a non-advertised cache expense.

Compaction is therefore an operation on the tail that is also an operation on the cache. You’re choosing to pay an invalidation cost today to stop paying rent tomorrow.

That’s the trade.

And before paying it, there are cheaper places to intervene.

The ladder

There are five moves against tail growth. They aren’t alternatives so much as rungs. The higher you climb, the more existing history you are willing to disturb.

One: don’t generate it. Cap the output at the tool. Anthropic’s text editor tool supports max_characters , web search supports max_uses. Codex caps individual tool outputs betwen 10,000 — 16,000 tokens by default, before they reach the compaction calculation. The more disciplined version is snipping. Keep a head and a tail, trim the middle, on the assumption that what a command started with and where it ended matter more than the scroll back between them.

The weakness is that you’re truncating before you know what mattered. A stack trace with the relevant frame removed is worse than no stack trace.

Two, spill it. Don’t carry the whole observation if you don’t need the whole observation. When a tool result crosses a size threshold, the harness can write it to disk and leave a reference behind. The full artifact survives, the live context doesn’t.

This is different from truncation. Nothing was thrown away. A 500k-line build log or terminal result can live on disk while the context contains only its path, metadata, or a searchable index. When the agent needs something from it later, a native search or read tool pulls back only the relevant slice.

Keep the artifact. Remove the observation.

This is one of the cleanest ways to separate storage from context. The information remains durable without collecting rent on every subsequent turn.

The catch is that the harness needs the tools to find it again. Spill-to-disk only works if the agent can search, read, and reason about what it stored. Otherwise you’ve traded context overflow for a filesystem full of things that can’t be retrieve.

The convergence here is striking. Several harnesses land on nearly the same threshold. Claude Code spills any tool result over roughly a 100k to disk and hands back a preview plus a path. Hermes uses the same 100k per-result cap. And both make the same pointed exception, the read tool is exempt from spilling, because a spilled read is a path that the agent would only read again. Literally, a read to spill to read, forever. I honestly have gone into infinite loops here. Be careful. The one tool whose whole job is to pull content back is the one tool you must never spill.

Three, don’t admit it. Delegate the work. A subagent with the harnesses native tools can read the files, scan the logs, explore the repository, and accumulate a large working context without any of that history entering the parent’s tail. When the task ends, the child’s window disappears and only its return value crosses the boundary.

This is genuinely one of the most popular features harnesses shipped this year. However, exploration is not as dangerous as modification. A worker that reads the wrong files costs you a re-run. A worker that edits the wrong files leaves damage behind after its context is gone. Be careful about which model you allow to do a modification. Back in the day, a scout wasn’t typically a high-ranked officer of your kingdom. You sent someone fast and expendable to go look. Looking is cheap and the report is easy to check. An emperor looking to overtake would always send their best to do the taking, the act itself is the thing that can’t be undone.

Delegate the scouting to a cheap, disposable context. Reserve your strongest for the move that actually changes the world. And, keep the parent in the loop to verify it.

The parent pays for the answer, not the investigation.

Four, replace it with a pointer. If the content already exists durably — a file, artifact, generated report, or spilled tool result — the pointer is all the conversation needs. A re-read goes back to where the content lives without carrying the content permanently in the conversation.

Anthropic’s memory tool is exactly this, built for you. OpenAI provides similar behavior with their Tools API (Function Calling).

Turn expensive conversational state into a cheap reference to durable state.

The model platform determines how much of this machinery the harness has to build itself.

Anthropic (compaction docs) provides two distinct forms of help, and they solve different problems. clear_tool_uses_20250919 is surgical once the prompt crosses a threshold — 100k input tokens by default, keeping the three most recent tool uses — it clears stale tool results server-side and replaces each with a placeholder. clear_at_least is the amortization knob, forcing you to specify a floor worth the invalidation. compact_20260112 is the heavier primitive, full server-side summarization, a new representation of the conversation rather than a removal from the old one.

Claude Code is particularly instructive because even the harness built by the company providing those primitives still appears to orchestrate its heavier /compact behavior itself — based on community reverse-engineering (barazany.dev and karanprasad.com, both tracing to the same Github sourced exposure) rather than Anthropic’s public documentation. The light clearing rides server-side. The actual /compact, the operation that decides what conversational state survives, is a client-orchestrated call.

OpenAI’s server-side offering is centered on compaction. /v1/responses/compact returns an opaque, encrypted blob the client passes back without inspecting — encrypted in part to close off a prompt-injection surface, a tampered summary steering later turns. There’s no OpenAI equivalent of surgical clearing, so Codex still has to manage tool-output size itself, and underneath both paths sits a crude fallback exceed the window anyway and Codex just drops the oldest history item and retries.

DeepSeek provides much less context-management machinery. Its server-side prefix caching is a cost optimization, not a solution to the fixed-window problem — a harness operating there has to own the entire compression pipeline itself. The official DeepSeek Harness builds one, and does it non-destructively shadowed events stay in the log and stay reachable. A third-party DeepSeek TUI I looked at doesn’t bother, and simply doesn’t proactively compact at all.

The interesting point isn’t which API has the best compaction endpoint. It’s where the responsibility for deciding what survives lives.

Hermes is useful as the limiting example because it operates across multiple providers. It can’t assume any one platform will provide the necessary primitives, so it runs its own client-side compressor as the floor — a dual-threshold design, 50% from its own token accounting, 85% from a rougher gateway-level check that catches sessions accumulating between turns while nobody’s watching and reaches past that compressor whenever the active provider offers something better.

That’s the right general architecture. The harness should own the compression by default, they have information a server may never see. Then, defer to the platform when the platform earns it.

Because regardless of who performs the fold, the same question remains.

What are you willing to forget?
Coming back to camp

Everything above assumed the session never stops.

But sessions stop. The laptop closes. The process dies. The CI job exits. Someone types /resume and expects to pick up where they left off.

It’s the easiest thing you’ll type all day for the most expensive turn in the session. /resume is seven characters, counting the slash, same shape as /help or /clear — no arguments, no confirmation, no friction. Nothing about it says what it costs, and the interface has one job here, which is pure convenience, so it’s tuned to make coming back feel free.

The conversation can come back. The cache cannot.

A resumed session is not a paused process. The harness replays the transcript from disk and reconstructs the message history. The conversation returns from durable storage, but the warm prefix does not.

That creates two different kinds of recovery.

The first is economic. As discussed in Part 2, Anthropic’s prefix cache has a TTL — five minutes by default, an hour if you paid the heavier write for it — refreshed only by activity. A resume is idle time taken to its limit, a gap with no process on the other end at all. So the prefix that had been cheap to reuse comes back stone cold, and the next turn pays full price to re-establish it. The most expensive cost is resuming a multiple day long-session, so be aware and smart with how you manage your sessions.

The second is informational. If the transcript is larger than the available window, the harness may have to fold it before the first new action happens. And that’s a particularly dangerous fold — the session is being compressed before you’ve had a chance to re-establish what matters. A constraint that explained a decision nine turns ago may be present in the transcript but absent from the compressed representation. The agent resumes with a smaller window and a plausible history, but not necessarily the history that made the previous decisions make sense.

What survives a fold is what survives a resume. That’s the deeper reason durable state matters. Project-root rules can be re-injected from disk. Files can be read again. A todo list can be reconstructed. A generated build log can be stored and referenced. But a conversation-only decision has no external source. If it survives only because the transcript carried it, it must be paid for again when the session comes back. If it was folded away, it may simply be gone.

The hierarchy is therefore not just about cost. It’s about durability.

Created with matplotlib. reconstructable state → durable external state → live conversational state → ephemeral observations.

The closer something is to the bottom, the more vulnerable it is to a fold.

Where folding breaks

There are two ways folding fails.

The acute failure is obvious. Compaction succeeds. A huge tool output immediately refills the window. The harness compacts again. The same output arrives. The harness compacts again, like a machine bailing the boat while drilling the hole.

Claude Code stops retrying rather than burning calls in a loop, baked in logic to identify when its in a loop and agent isn’t progressing. That’s the right behavior. But the loop itself is the signal. You’re operating on the wrong rung. Ideally, it should self-reflect to identify a different approach rather than retrying a native tool. If the same oversized file keeps forcing compaction, the answer isn’t a lower threshold. It’s a line-range read, a scoped grep, a pointer to durable output, or a subagent whose window you don’t need to preserve. (Note to readers, Claude Code has multiple Stop Iterations called at different sites, I am not referring to /goal or /loop here).

Every time you find yourself tuning compaction, ask whether the answer is three rungs up or a different approach entirely.

The chronic failure is more interesting. Compaction is lossy, and long sessions don’t compact once. They compact. Work. Compact again. Work. Compact again. Summaries of summaries of summaries.

Folds of folds

The first fold can be excellent and still create a bad third fold. Because the second summarizer isn’t looking at the original history. It’s looking at a representation chosen by the first summarizer. The third isn’t looking at either of those, it’s looking at the second summarizer’s judgment about the first summarizer’s judgment.

That changes what information is at risk. The original conversation contains both facts and reasons. The first fold may preserve, “we chose approach B.” The second may preserve, “approach B is the current implementation.” The third may preserve, “current implementation uses approach B.”

All three statements are true. But the reason approach A was rejected has disappeared. The system hasn’t forgotten the decision. It has forgotten the information that made the decision intelligible. That’s the distinctive failure of folds of folds.

Created with matplotlib. Should this be persisted into memory architectures as an entity-relationship structure?What should survive?

Across different harnesses, structured summaries keep converging on roughly the same categories:

  • Intention, what are we trying to accomplish?
  • State, what have we learned or changed?
  • Work/ To-dos, what has been completed and what remains?
  • Open items, what is unresolved, constrained, or still under consideration?

Different harnesses give these fields different names, but the shape keeps recurring. Maybe that’s the smallest practical state a session needs to preserve. Several harnesses also have file restoration techniques to minify stale / cached file reads post-compaction. Claude Code, Hermes, and DeepSeek Harness all keep a small record of what was read, keyed on path + range + modification time (mtime), and return a lightweight stub instead of re-sending a file whose contents haven’t changed. The read already happened, its just, the tokens don’t have to happen again.

But even that isn’t enough if those fields themselves are repeatedly summarized without a durable source of truth. A summary can say “we decided to use approach B.” A durable artifact can say “we decided to use approach B because constraint X makes approach A invalid.” The second survives compression better because the reason exists somewhere outside the compression process.

That’s the bridge from compaction to memory.

Memory is what survives the fold

The obvious response to lossy compression is to compress better. The more durable response is to move important information somewhere that doesn’t need to be compressed with the conversation at all. I will write more on this later, but let’s leave it here for now.

This is why memory tooling matters. This is why companies have all defined their own paths forward towards memory architectures, and have previously wrote about Memory Engineering.

Anthropic’s context-editing and memory mechanisms make the boundary explicit. aA the conversation approaches a clearing threshold, the agent can be given an opportunity to write important state to durable memory before volatile context is removed. The techniques we mentioned above, can be repurposed.

The system is effectively saying, “you’re about to forget this, write down what matters.”

That’s a fundamentally different operation from asking the model to summarize everything. A summary tries to make the live window smaller. Memory tries to make some information independent of the live window. And that distinction becomes more important with every fold.

The ideal long-running harness therefore isn’t one that never compacts. It’s one that understands the difference between information that can be regenerated, information that can be referenced, information that should be compressed, and information that must survive unchanged.

The last category shouldn’t depend on a summary of a summary. It should have somewhere else to live.

The long climb

Never invalidating the cache is a fairytale. A fixed context window eventually forces a fold. The invalidation cost is unavoidable. The smaller window is the mechanical outcome.

But that isn’t the hard problem. The hard problem is deciding what gets carried to the next camp. And then the camp after that. And the camp after that.

A long-running agent isn’t maintaining one context window. It’s maintaining a sequence of compressed representations of its own history. History becomes summary. Summary becomes memory. Memory becomes the input to the next summary. Every fold is therefore a judgment about what the agent is allowed to forget.

The engineering challenge isn’t to make the pack infinitely large. It’s to make sure the things that matter aren’t the things left at camp.

Harnesses, Part One: Eager vs. Just-in-Time and Part Two, Cache Economics are on Medium, Towards Data Science.

items.title: Why Pepsi's surprise $1.7 billion Publicis deal has Madison Avenue reeling
items.summary: Kevin Carter/Getty Images A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter . Forget the Jets and the Sharks, the Yankees and the Red Sox, or Arsenal v. Spurs (on my side of the pond). Few rivalries run as deep as Coca-Cola and Pepsi . That explains why Madison Avenue was so stunned by last week's news: Publicis Groupe had won PepsiCo's $1.7 billion global media, data, and tech account without a traditional pitch. (Omnicom was Pepsi's global media partner for more than 25 years, though Publicis media agencies did already work with the beverage and snacks giant in some markets in Asia.) The context: Publicis handles Coca-Cola's media in North America — and was competing against incumbent WPP for Coke's global business. "I was gobsmacked and shellshocked all week," one marketing consultant told me. Another sent me an unprintable expletive. Two people familiar with the matter told me Publicis has withdrawn from Coke's global pitch and is set to resign the North America account — a business it had won from WPP last year. The Coke North America business is estimated to be worth $805 million, while the global business amounts to $1.8 billion in spending, per the research company COMvergence. AdAge reported on Tuesday that Coke is now planning to put its North American media business back under review. Publicis' coup is widely viewed as a masterstroke by Arthur Sadoun's company , which similarly clinched Microsoft's media business in April without a formal pitch. It also shows how consolidation of the agency landscape is reshaping CMOs' options — particularly for marketers who demand category exclusivity. Madison Avenue's review culture When Coca-Cola confirmed its global media review in June, Pepsi's marketing team quickly seized the opportunity to strike before it was too late. If Publicis had won Coke, Pepsi would have had few obvious alternatives to retaining Omnicom as its global media partner. WPP and Publicis' relationship with Coke would have made those agencies off-limits, and Omnicom's acquisition of IPG , as well as Dentsu's international struggles , left few other scaled global media operations in the market for a company of PepsiCo's size. "Top-to-top dealmaking is getting more prevalent vis-a-vis running a process with guarantees on people, remuneration, and media cost," said Ruben Schreurs, CEO of the marketing consultancy Ebiquity. "Is this a sign of the times to come?" It's an embarrassing blow for Coke, which had been expecting to convene leaders from Publicis and WPP in Mexico City this week in the latest stage of the global media pitch. Only WPP made it. Reviews are costly and time-consuming for both agencies and clients: WPP and Publicis execs had already flown to Shanghai and London as part of the process. Some major global advertisers deem these lengthy processes necessary as they make major decisions over which agencies are best equipped to handle their billions of dollars in ad spending. It's not just about which agency has the most persuasive "pitch" and charismatic leaders in the presentation room. Advertisers and their procurement teams can spend months, and even years, haggling on pricing, the top people who will be assigned to their accounts, and stress-testing agencies' capabilities in areas such as data, tech, commerce media, and increasingly AI. Volkswagen's global media review memorably stretched over three years before it reappointed Omnicom's PHD in 2024. Given all the complexity involved in such reviews, industry insiders said they were surprised that Publicis' move came as the Coke review was well underway. "It couldn't have been more shocking in a more shocking category with two more shocking brands at a more shocking point in the process," an agency head told me. items.title: Gap taps a new exec to find its next act beyond fashion
items.summary: Jamie Drew, Gap Inc.'s new head of strategic partnerships and growth, wants to move Gap beyond apparel. Gap Inc. Gap Inc. just made a big hire to help the company move beyond clothes. Jamie Drew will seek out partnerships and new businesses in areas that could include travel, sports, and gaming. Gap has made notable forays into music, but it's risky for brands to go into non-core areas. Gap Inc. wants to be in the middle of the cultural conversation — and just tapped a new exec to grow its business beyond clothes. Gap has hired Jamie Drew as its new head of strategic partnerships and growth, reporting to chief entertainment officer Pam Kaufman, the company exclusively told Business Insider. Drew is tasked with helping push Gap's brands — including Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Athleta, as well as Gap — beyond apparel to other consumer touchpoints. Her mandate is to look beyond traditional fashion partnerships to areas where the parent company or its individual brands could reach new audiences and create new businesses. The company said those areas could include experiences and destinations, hospitality or travel, sports and fitness communities, gaming, and food and beverage. Drew was most recently EVP of consumer products and experiences at Paramount Global, also Kaufman's alma mater, following 15 years at its kids channel Nickelodeon. She helped build the kids' franchise Paw Patrol into a retail business, acquire Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, take SpongeBob SquarePants to Broadway, and open the first Nickelodeon Hotel. Drew said her most successful initiatives embodied the brand's DNA. "Brand partnerships only work when they're truly authentic to the brand's ethos and extend its consumer relevance," she said. Reimagining Gap has been a top priority for Richard Dickson, who has revived the retail giant since becoming CEO in 2023. This year, Gap tapped Kaufman for its first chief entertainment role, Walmart alum Justin Breton to drive original content, and Paramount alum Lourdes Arocho to head up licensing. Gap has made headlines for its cultural marketing The company has already been inserting itself into culture — and the Gap brand is its star. Over the past year, the Gap brand has tapped into celebrities and cultural events to draw attention. It cast global pop girl group Katseye in an ad, produced a video with Puerto Rican artist Young Miko around Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show, became Coachella's exclusive apparel sponsor and merch partner, and dropped a buzzy collection of jeans with Hailey Bieber. Meanwhile, Banana Republic is bringing back nostalgia with refurbished vintage styles. Old Navy has also been working with stars like Paris Hilton and influencer Haylee Baylee, and launched a collection of clothes with luxury designer Christopher John Rogers. Gap Inc. also launched a loyalty program with exclusive drops and other benefits. Working with influencers and outside designers has been a frequent strategy for big retailers. J.Crew, for instance, worked with several designers to reimagine one of its classic sweater styles and cast internet star Emma Chamberlain for its latest collection. Other consumer brands have gotten creative, too, by moving beyond selling products over the years. Nike and Ralph Lauren are experimenting with cafés and dining, Lululemon acquired fitness company Mirror, and JPMorgan Chase bought food review site The Infatuation to give customers dining-related perks. Jumping into new areas can be risky Brands have to be careful about launching extensions or moving into new areas where there's stiff competition or the brand doesn't add any new value, though, said Kevin Lane Keller, a marketing professor at Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business. Such moves have worked for some, like Ralph Lauren, whose defined brand translated well into home decor, but there have been some notable flops, like McDonald's foray into luxury hotels in the 2000s. The Gap brand had a yearslong revenue slump before Dickson's arrival, which it attributed in part to having too many products and styles. That history could impair Gap's ability to take more than small steps, Keller said. "Over time, if you haven't carved out a strong identity and reinforced it, that's not going to make it easy to move into unrelated categories," he said. "They also haven't stretched out of apparel that much." Gap may be about to face the first test of its ability to extend its brand, having just made a concerted push into accessories under the leadership of Coach alum Reed Krakoff. items.title: Boston Scientific  - Cyberattack having "material impact" on annual income
items.summary: Biotech and medical equipment manufacturer Boston Scientific will no longer meet financial targets this year after a cyberattack in August, it revealed in an SEC filing on Tuesday. The company is still recovering certain systems after the attack, identified on August 25 , and subsequent network outage, and said it determined the fallout would have a “material impact” on its Q3 and full year earnings. The Form 8-K document said the outage temporarily “impacted the company’s ability to manufacture as well as process and ship customer orders” and would affect its bottom line despite the company having recovered most operations already. While Boston Scientific said it was yet to determine the full impact, it said it will not meet the 3-5% growth it projected for net sales Q3 in its July Q2 earnings, or the 5-6.5% growth projected for its full year earnings. The company recorded $5.4 billion in net sales for Q2 and will provide another update with its Q3 earnings release in October. Cyberattacks in healthcare
items.summary_html:
Biotech and medical equipment manufacturer Boston Scientific will no longer meet financial targets this year after a cyberattack in August, it revealed in an SEC filing on Tuesday.

The company is still recovering certain systems after the attack, identified on August 25, and subsequent network outage, and said it determined the fallout would have a “material impact” on its Q3 and full year earnings.

The Form 8-K document said the outage temporarily “impacted the company’s ability to manufacture as well as process and ship customer orders” and would affect its bottom line despite the company having recovered most operations already.

While Boston Scientific said it was yet to determine the full impact, it said it will not meet the 3-5% growth it projected for net sales Q3 in its July Q2 earnings, or the 5-6.5% growth projected for its full year earnings.

The company recorded $5.4 billion in net sales for Q2 and will provide another update with its Q3 earnings release in October.

items.summary_html:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

What OpenAI’s latest controversy tells us about the future of math

OpenAI says its agents have solved one of the most important open problems in mathematics. Under normal circumstances, that would be a huge milestone. But the announcement has been overshadowed by accusations that OpenAI failed to credit researchers whose AI-assisted work influenced its solution.

Whether those accusations are true or not, the episode may mark a turning point in the history of mathematics. AI models now seem essential for making progress on the field’s most important problems, but solving them may demand resources available only to a couple of frontier AI companies.

If that’s the future we are headed for, it is unclear how human mathematicians will fit into it.

Read on to see how AI could reshape mathematics.

—Grace Huckins

Batteries just broke another record in the US

Battery installations hit a new record in the US in the second quarter of 2026, with 20.2 gigawatt-hours of new capacity coming online. That’s enough to supply the daily electricity needs of 600,000 homes.

The surge puts the country on track for another record year, driven by cheaper batteries and an urgent need for more energy storage as renewables are added to the grid. But the boom looks different for grid-scale and residential batteries.

Take a closer look at the forces reshaping the US battery market.

—Casey Crownhart

This entrepreneur is developing agents that can plan ahead

Danijar Hafner’s office in San Francisco’s SoMa district sits mostly empty, but what it lacks in decor, it makes up for in robots. Humanoids of various shapes and sizes hang like marionettes from racks that run down the center of the wide-open space.

Hafner won’t say too much about his new venture just yet, but describes it as a continuation of his longtime work to enable AI to navigate environments it has not encountered in training.

Over the years, the 31-year-old has honed his approach by pitting agents trained within his world models against popular video games. More recently, he’s begun migrating his agents out of the virtual world and into physical reality.

Learn more about Hafner’s work teaching AI about our world.

—Mat Honan

Danijar Hafner is one of the artificial intelligence honorees on our 35 Innovators Under 35 list for 2026. Meet the rest of them here, or explore the full list across the biotechnology, AI, computing and robotics, and climate and energy categories.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace

Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones. But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector: the data those drones generate.

Ukraine has begun making millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to military contractors and commercial companies. It’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships, but it turns the front line into a model training site, using the chaos of war to create conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce.

As this new industry takes shape, we need a regulatory system that ensures battlefield data isn’t treated like ordinary commercial material.


This is our latest article to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

It used 10,000 AI agents to tackle the Navier-Stokes equations. (CNBC)

+ Targeting Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok, among others. (NBC News)

3 The Pentagon asked OpenAI for an AI model that rarely says no
The military wanted it to have “minimal refusal rates.” (Intercept)
+ The Pentagon says US allies can’t keep pace on AI. (Guardian)
+ AI firms may soon train on classified military data. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Apple is expected to unveil a $2,000 folding smartphone today
It would be the iPhone’s biggest design change since its 2007 launch. (Guardian)
+ And the first big test for new CEO John Ternus. (NYT $)
+ Xiaomi and Huawei launched their own new foldables before the event. (CNBC)

5 Meta’s new AI agent can access apps to send emails and make payments
Muse autonomously uses apps and websites on people’s behalf. (CNBC)
+ Internal tests found it could expose sensitive personal data. (Reuters $)
+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)

New results will give more prominence to comparison sites. (Reuters $)

Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial will be released in the US on December 25. (Variety)

Quote of the day

—NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster issues a statement comparing OpenAI’s math breakthrough to an IBM supercomputer defeating chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, a landmark moment for machine intelligence.

One more thing


The shock of seeing your body used in deepfake porn

When Jennifer got a research job in 2023, she ran her new professional headshot through a facial recognition program. She wanted to see whether it would pull up the porn videos she’d made more than a decade earlier. It did, but it also surfaced something she’d never seen before: one of her old videos, now featuring someone else’s face on her body.

Conversations about sexualized deepfakes usually focus on the people whose faces are inserted into explicit content without consent. But another group often gets ignored: the people whose bodies those faces are attached to.

items.title: Why Is Your LLM Recomputing the Same Prompt 1,000 Times a Day?
items.summary: Prefix caching, radix trees and block hashing explained TL; DR Real LLM traffic is enormously repetitive. System prompts, chat history and shared documents mean requests overlap heavily at the start. Attention is causal, so a token’s cached state depends only on the tokens before it. Two requests with an identical prefix produce an identical cache for that prefix. Prefix caching keeps that state after a request finishes so the next request can reuse it, skipping prefill entirely for the shared portion. vLLM identifies reusable state by hashing each cache block together with the hash of everything before it . SGLang organises the same information as a radix tree . The gain shows up as lower time-to-first-token and reclaimed prefill capacity — often dramatic for long shared prompts. The cost is memory: blocks kept for future reuse are blocks unavailable to active requests. Here is a pattern that shows up in almost every production LLM deployment. An application has a system prompt — instructions, tone, policy, tool definitions, maybe a few examples. It might be 4,000 tokens. Every single request begins with it. The user’s actual question is 20 tokens on the end. So the server processes those 4,000 tokens. Then the next request arrives and it processes the same 4,000 tokens again. Then again. A thousand times an hour, computing an identical result and discarding it each time. This article is about why that happens, why it is fixable, and how modern inference engines fix it. 1. First, what gets recomputed A quick definition, because the rest depends on it. When a model processes text, each token produces a key and a value vector at every layer. Generating subsequent tokens requires the keys and values of everything before them, so the engine stores that state rather than recomputing it. This store is the KV cache , and building it for the input prompt is the prefill phase — the work done before the first output token appears. Prefill is expensive and scales with prompt length. For a large model, processing several thousand prompt tokens can take a noticeable fraction of a second, and that time lands directly on the user’s time-to-first-token. Normally, when a request finishes, its cache is released and the state is gone. That is the behaviour we are about to question. 2. Real traffic overlaps far more than you would expect Repeated prefixes are not a corner case. They are the dominant shape of production traffic. System prompts. Every request from an application carries the same instruction block. Often thousands of tokens, identical every time. Multi-turn conversations. Models are stateless. Turn five of a chat re-sends turns one through four in full. The prefix of each turn is the entire conversation so far — and it was computed on the previous turn. Shared documents. In retrieval and document-analysis workloads, many users ask different questions against the same document. The document is the prefix. Few-shot examples. Prompts with fixed demonstrations before the variable part. In workloads like these the shared portion is frequently the large majority of the prompt. 3. Why reuse is possible at all The overlap alone does not justify reuse. What justifies it is a property of how attention works. Attention in a generative model is causal : a token can attend to the tokens before it, never to the tokens after. Which means a token’s key and value depend only on itself and on everything preceding it — and on nothing that follows. Casual Attention and Prefix cache Reuse The consequence is exact and worth stating carefully: If two requests begin with the identical sequence of tokens, the KV cache for that shared portion is identical — regardless of what either request contains afterwards. Nothing appended later can retroactively change it. That is what makes the state safely reusable rather than merely similar. Note the strictness. The prefix must match from the very first token , and it must match exactly. Shared text in the middle of two prompts is not reusable, because the state at that position depends on the different text preceding it. Prefix caching earns its name precisely. 4. What a cache hit actually buys Suppose an application has a 4,000-token system prompt and users send short questions. Without prefix caching, every request prefills 4,020 tokens. With it, the first request prefills 4,020 and each subsequent one prefills roughly 20 — the shared 4,000 are read from cache. Two things improve, and they are worth separating. Time to first token drops sharply. Prefill was the dominant term for the request; almost all of it disappears. To put rough numbers on it: if a deployment prefills at a few thousand tokens per second, those 4,000 shared tokens were costing on the order of a second of TTFT on every request, before the model even looked at the user’s question. A hit removes nearly all of it. For long shared prompts this is the difference between a sluggish interface and an immediate one. Prefill capacity is reclaimed. The GPU cycles that were being spent recomputing identical state become available for real work. Across a busy server this raises throughput even for requests that never hit the cache. The saving scales with how much of the prompt is shared. A 100-token system prompt is not worth much. A 20,000-token document that fifty users are querying is worth an enormous amount. 5. The unit of reuse is a block Modern engines do not store a sequence’s cache as one contiguous region. They split it into fixed-size blocks , each holding a set number of tokens — 16 is a common default — allocated on demand. That choice, made originally to avoid wasting memory, turns out to be exactly what prefix caching needs. Reuse operates at block granularity: a block is either identical to one already in memory, or it is not. The practical consequence is that reuse is block-aligned . If two prompts share 4,005 tokens and the block size is 16, the engine can reuse the first 250 complete blocks — 4,000 tokens — and recomputes the partial remainder. A trivial rounding loss, but it explains why matches are reported in blocks rather than exact token counts. 6. How the engine recognises a reusable block This is the mechanism at the centre of the article. The engine needs to answer one question quickly: have I already computed the state for this exact block, in this exact position, with this exact history? All three conditions matter. A hash of just the block’s own tokens is not enough. The same 16 tokens appearing at the start of one prompt and in the middle of another have completely different state, because the state depends on everything preceding them. Hashing only the contents would produce a false match and silently corrupt the output. So vLLM chains the hashes . Each block’s hash is computed from its own tokens together with the hash of the preceding block : Chained Block Hashes for KV Cache Reuse Each hash therefore identifies not “these 16 tokens” but “these 16 tokens, arrived at through exactly this history.” Two blocks match only if their entire preceding sequence matched, which is precisely the condition that makes reuse correct. Those hashes go into a lookup table pointing at physical blocks. When a request arrives, the engine hashes its prompt block by block and looks each one up. 7. Matching stops at the first difference Lookup walks forward from the first block and stops as soon as one misses. Cached:  [ A ][ B ][ C ][ D ][ E ] New:     [ A ][ B ][ C ][ X ][ Y ] ✓    ✓    ✓    ✗ └── reused ──┘ └ computed ┘ This is exactly the behaviour multi-turn chat needs. Each new turn shares every block of the conversation so far and diverges only at the newly appended message. The reused portion grows with the conversation, so prefill cost per turn stays roughly flat instead of climbing with history length. It also answers the question in this article’s title. When a deployment has prefix caching enabled and is still recomputing everything, the cause is almost always variable content at the front of the prompt. A timestamp, session ID, user name or A/B flag injected at the top of an otherwise-fixed system prompt changes block 0 — which changes hash₀, which changes every hash downstream, which destroys every match for the entire prompt. One dynamic line at the top can cost you the other four thousand tokens. The fix is mechanical: put stable content first, variable content last. Fixed instructions, tool definitions and examples at the top; anything that changes per request at the bottom. 8. A different structure: radix trees vLLM’s hash table is one way to organise this. SGLang takes another, called RadixAttention . A radix tree stores strings by shared prefix: common beginnings become shared branches, and divergence creates a fork. Applied to token sequences, the cached prefixes form a tree where each path from the root is a cached sequence, and any shared prefix is stored once on a shared path. RadixAttention Shared Prefix Tree Both approaches answer the same question and both evict with LRU. The difference is structural: a hash table gives direct lookup of a known block, while a tree makes the relationships between cached prefixes explicit — you can see which sequences share what, which branches are hot, and where a new request would attach. SGLang uses that visibility for cache-aware scheduling, ordering requests to maximise reuse. For a practitioner the takeaway is not which is better. It is that both engines cache prefixes, both evict LRU, and both benefit from the same prompt structure. 9. Eviction, and why this is cheaper than it sounds Cached prefixes cannot be kept forever. Memory is finite and the pool is shared with active requests. The elegant part of the design is that a finished request’s blocks are not immediately wiped. They are marked free and left in place. If a new request hashes to them before they are needed elsewhere, it gets a hit at no cost. If memory pressure arrives first, they are reclaimed, least-recently-used first. items.summary_html:
Prefix caching, radix trees and block hashing explained
TL; DR
Real LLM traffic is enormously repetitive. System prompts, chat history and shared documents mean requests overlap heavily at the start.
Attention is causal, so a token’s cached state depends only on the tokens before it. Two requests with an identical prefix produce an identical cache for that prefix.
Prefix caching keeps that state after a request finishes so the next request can reuse it, skipping prefill entirely for the shared portion.
vLLM identifies reusable state by hashing each cache block together with the hash of everything before it. SGLang organises the same information as a radix tree.
The gain shows up as lower time-to-first-token and reclaimed prefill capacity — often dramatic for long shared prompts.
The cost is memory: blocks kept for future reuse are blocks unavailable to active requests.

Here is a pattern that shows up in almost every production LLM deployment.

An application has a system prompt — instructions, tone, policy, tool definitions, maybe a few examples. It might be 4,000 tokens. Every single request begins with it. The user’s actual question is 20 tokens on the end.

So the server processes those 4,000 tokens. Then the next request arrives and it processes the same 4,000 tokens again. Then again. A thousand times an hour, computing an identical result and discarding it each time.

This article is about why that happens, why it is fixable, and how modern inference engines fix it.

1. First, what gets recomputed

A quick definition, because the rest depends on it.

When a model processes text, each token produces a key and a value vector at every layer. Generating subsequent tokens requires the keys and values of everything before them, so the engine stores that state rather than recomputing it. This store is the KV cache, and building it for the input prompt is the prefill phase — the work done before the first output token appears.

Prefill is expensive and scales with prompt length. For a large model, processing several thousand prompt tokens can take a noticeable fraction of a second, and that time lands directly on the user’s time-to-first-token.

Normally, when a request finishes, its cache is released and the state is gone. That is the behaviour we are about to question.

2. Real traffic overlaps far more than you would expect

Repeated prefixes are not a corner case. They are the dominant shape of production traffic.

System prompts. Every request from an application carries the same instruction block. Often thousands of tokens, identical every time.

Multi-turn conversations. Models are stateless. Turn five of a chat re-sends turns one through four in full. The prefix of each turn is the entire conversation so far — and it was computed on the previous turn.

Shared documents. In retrieval and document-analysis workloads, many users ask different questions against the same document. The document is the prefix.

Few-shot examples. Prompts with fixed demonstrations before the variable part.

In workloads like these the shared portion is frequently the large majority of the prompt.

3. Why reuse is possible at all

The overlap alone does not justify reuse. What justifies it is a property of how attention works.

Attention in a generative model is causal: a token can attend to the tokens before it, never to the tokens after. Which means a token’s key and value depend only on itself and on everything preceding it — and on nothing that follows.

Casual Attention and Prefix cache Reuse

The consequence is exact and worth stating carefully:

If two requests begin with the identical sequence of tokens, the KV cache for that shared portion is identical — regardless of what either request contains afterwards.

Nothing appended later can retroactively change it. That is what makes the state safely reusable rather than merely similar.

Note the strictness. The prefix must match from the very first token, and it must match exactly. Shared text in the middle of two prompts is not reusable, because the state at that position depends on the different text preceding it. Prefix caching earns its name precisely.

4. What a cache hit actually buys

Suppose an application has a 4,000-token system prompt and users send short questions.

Without prefix caching, every request prefills 4,020 tokens. With it, the first request prefills 4,020 and each subsequent one prefills roughly 20 — the shared 4,000 are read from cache.

Two things improve, and they are worth separating.

Time to first token drops sharply. Prefill was the dominant term for the request; almost all of it disappears. To put rough numbers on it: if a deployment prefills at a few thousand tokens per second, those 4,000 shared tokens were costing on the order of a second of TTFT on every request, before the model even looked at the user’s question. A hit removes nearly all of it. For long shared prompts this is the difference between a sluggish interface and an immediate one.

Prefill capacity is reclaimed. The GPU cycles that were being spent recomputing identical state become available for real work. Across a busy server this raises throughput even for requests that never hit the cache.

The saving scales with how much of the prompt is shared. A 100-token system prompt is not worth much. A 20,000-token document that fifty users are querying is worth an enormous amount.

5. The unit of reuse is a block

Modern engines do not store a sequence’s cache as one contiguous region. They split it into fixed-size blocks, each holding a set number of tokens — 16 is a common default — allocated on demand.

That choice, made originally to avoid wasting memory, turns out to be exactly what prefix caching needs. Reuse operates at block granularity: a block is either identical to one already in memory, or it is not.

The practical consequence is that reuse is block-aligned. If two prompts share 4,005 tokens and the block size is 16, the engine can reuse the first 250 complete blocks — 4,000 tokens — and recomputes the partial remainder. A trivial rounding loss, but it explains why matches are reported in blocks rather than exact token counts.

6. How the engine recognises a reusable block

This is the mechanism at the centre of the article.

The engine needs to answer one question quickly: have I already computed the state for this exact block, in this exact position, with this exact history? All three conditions matter.

A hash of just the block’s own tokens is not enough. The same 16 tokens appearing at the start of one prompt and in the middle of another have completely different state, because the state depends on everything preceding them. Hashing only the contents would produce a false match and silently corrupt the output.

So vLLM chains the hashes. Each block’s hash is computed from its own tokens together with the hash of the preceding block:

Chained Block Hashes for KV Cache Reuse

Each hash therefore identifies not “these 16 tokens” but “these 16 tokens, arrived at through exactly this history.” Two blocks match only if their entire preceding sequence matched, which is precisely the condition that makes reuse correct.

Those hashes go into a lookup table pointing at physical blocks. When a request arrives, the engine hashes its prompt block by block and looks each one up.

7. Matching stops at the first difference

Lookup walks forward from the first block and stops as soon as one misses.

Cached:  [ A ][ B ][ C ][ D ][ E ]
New:     [ A ][ B ][ C ][ X ][ Y ]
           ✓    ✓    ✓    ✗
         └── reused ──┘ └ computed ┘

This is exactly the behaviour multi-turn chat needs. Each new turn shares every block of the conversation so far and diverges only at the newly appended message. The reused portion grows with the conversation, so prefill cost per turn stays roughly flat instead of climbing with history length.

It also answers the question in this article’s title. When a deployment has prefix caching enabled and is still recomputing everything, the cause is almost always variable content at the front of the prompt. A timestamp, session ID, user name or A/B flag injected at the top of an otherwise-fixed system prompt changes block 0 — which changes hash₀, which changes every hash downstream, which destroys every match for the entire prompt. One dynamic line at the top can cost you the other four thousand tokens.

The fix is mechanical: put stable content first, variable content last. Fixed instructions, tool definitions and examples at the top; anything that changes per request at the bottom.

8. A different structure: radix trees

vLLM’s hash table is one way to organise this. SGLang takes another, called RadixAttention.

A radix tree stores strings by shared prefix: common beginnings become shared branches, and divergence creates a fork. Applied to token sequences, the cached prefixes form a tree where each path from the root is a cached sequence, and any shared prefix is stored once on a shared path.

RadixAttention Shared Prefix Tree

Both approaches answer the same question and both evict with LRU. The difference is structural: a hash table gives direct lookup of a known block, while a tree makes the relationships between cached prefixes explicit — you can see which sequences share what, which branches are hot, and where a new request would attach. SGLang uses that visibility for cache-aware scheduling, ordering requests to maximise reuse.

For a practitioner the takeaway is not which is better. It is that both engines cache prefixes, both evict LRU, and both benefit from the same prompt structure.

9. Eviction, and why this is cheaper than it sounds

Cached prefixes cannot be kept forever. Memory is finite and the pool is shared with active requests.

The elegant part of the design is that a finished request’s blocks are not immediately wiped. They are marked free and left in place. If a new request hashes to them before they are needed elsewhere, it gets a hit at no cost. If memory pressure arrives first, they are reclaimed, least-recently-used first.

So prefix caching largely runs on memory that would otherwise sit idle. It does not reserve a separate pool; it defers cleanup. That is why engines can enable it by default — in the common case it costs nothing and sometimes saves a great deal.

The cost appears under pressure. When the server is saturated, blocks retained for possible reuse are blocks unavailable to active sequences, so the engine faces a real trade-off between memory for reuse and memory for concurrency. Hot, highly-shared workloads want more retention; workloads with unique prompts want none.

10. When it does not help

Prefix caching is close to free, but it is not universal.

Unique prompts. Workloads where every request is genuinely different get nothing. All lookups miss, and the retained blocks are pure overhead.

Variable content at the front. The single most common reason a cache appears to do nothing — see Section 7.

Cache too small for the working set. If the hot prefixes exceed available memory, entries are evicted before they are reused and the hit rate collapses.

Short prompts. Saving a few hundred tokens of prefill is not material.

Decode is untouched. Prefix caching removes redundant prefill. Generation still runs one token at a time, at the same speed. A request that spends most of its time generating will barely notice a cache hit.

One operational note: because entries are keyed on token IDs, only genuinely identical content matches, and no content crosses between requests. What is observable is timing — hits are faster than misses. In shared multi-tenant deployments that is worth being aware of.

11. What to measure

Two numbers tell you whether this is working.

Prefix cache hit rate — the share of prompt blocks served from cache. Engines expose this directly. If it is near zero on a workload you expect to be repetitive, look for variable content at the front of your prompts before looking anywhere else.

TTFT, at p50 and p95 — hits and misses have very different profiles, so the average conceals the behaviour. A deployment with a high hit rate typically shows a fast median and a long tail of misses, and the gap between them is roughly what the cache is worth.

The next problem

Prefix caching changes the economics of a request in a way that has a consequence beyond the server it runs on.

Two identical requests no longer cost the same. One that lands where its prefix is cached skips almost all of its prefill and answers immediately. The same request landing elsewhere pays the full cost. The difference can be large.

Which is fine on a single server. It is not fine on twenty.

In a real deployment, traffic arrives at a load balancer sitting in front of many replicas, and each replica has its own cache holding its own set of prefixes. Those caches are not shared. Server A may hold the state for a request that would be nearly free to serve there — while a round-robin balancer, knowing nothing about any of this, sends it to Server B to be computed from scratch, evicting something useful in the process.

And cached state is only part of it. LLM requests were never interchangeable to begin with. A 200-token prompt with a 20-token answer costs almost nothing. A 30,000-token prompt with a 4,000-token answer occupies a large share of a server’s memory for a long time. A load balancer counting connections cannot tell them apart, and counts them the same.

So the routing layer is making decisions about wildly unequal work, with no idea where the valuable state lives.

What would a load balancer have to know about an inference server to route to it well?

That is the next layer of the stack.

The series

2. What Do You Do With a Model That’s Too Big for Your GPU? — Quantization, Sharding and Parallelism Explained

3. How Does One GPU Serve Hundreds of Users at the Same Time? — Inside an LLM inference server

4. The KV Cache Explained: Why Long Conversations Get Expensive — How LLMs remember context without recomputing everything

5. Why Is Your LLM Recomputing the Same Prompt 1,000 Times a Day? — Prefix caching, radix trees and block hashing explained

6. Why Traditional Load Balancing Breaks for LLMs — Building an LLM-aware router
(Next Article)

7. Kubernetes for LLM Inference: How AI Workloads Run Across a GPU Cluster

8. LLM-D Explained — How modern AI infrastructure routes, schedules and scales LLM inference

9. Inside a Modern AI Inference Platform — The full stack end-to-end

items.title: This startup raised $10 million to bring AI to old factories
items.summary: Harmoni cofounders David Caputo and Adam Ellis David Caputo and Adam Ellis Harmoni has raised $10 million from Bessemer Venture Partners to modernize factory floors. The funding comes as the US tries to reindustrialize after years of offshoring. Harmoni's new AI product, HAL, is designed to help workers automate routine tasks. Silicon Valley wants to build highly automated factories from scratch. This startup is betting on the ones America already has. Harmoni, which makes custom tablets and AI software for factory floors, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Bessemer Venture Partners, the company told Business Insider exclusively. It declined to disclose its valuation. Harmoni has around 40 customers and expects to add another 10 this month, with aerospace and defense making up its largest customer segment. The funding comes as the US tries to reindustrialize after years of offshoring. Some startups, including Hadrian and Machina Labs , are building new factories designed to rely heavily on robots and automation. Harmoni, by contrast, is targeting the roughly 280,000 American factories filled with traditional machinery and workers. "We've built this specifically to arm these guys to compete with these autonomous factories," cofounder David Caputo told Business Insider. Harmoni, which was founded in 2023, is competing in a crowded market where manufacturers already rely on a patchwork of software. Companies, including MachineMetrics and Datanomix, track machines and production, while other tools track workers, machine maintenance, and the steps required for specific jobs. Harmoni's pitch is that factories should not have to stitch all those systems together themselves — a problem Caputo and his cofounder, Adam Ellis, a longtime manufacturing consultant, said they repeatedly encountered while working with factories. At the center of Harmoni's system are custom tablets that attach magnetically to factory machines and can connect with equipment ranging from modern systems to machines built during World War II. Workers can use the tablets to clock in, pull up instructions, track jobs, and report problems from one place. A Harmoni tablet Harmoni Shokoufeh Mirzaei, chair and professor of industrial and manufacturing engineering at Cal Poly Pomona, said large companies like Amazon are far ahead on automation, while many small and midsize US factories lack basic analytics and run on technology that predates the internet. "We find the average factory is behind the automation curve and they use very old, legacy systems," Mirzaei told Business Insider. Many manufacturers are reluctant to replace expensive equipment, she said, but are open to retrofitting existing machines. 'Speak to the machines' Caputo first saw how much factory work remained manual more than a decade ago after leaving investment banking to start a firm that invests in manufacturers. The first time he walked a factory floor, he panicked. "I remember walking around the shop floor and thinking, 'Oh my God, I made a mistake,'" Caputo said. Workers were lining up to clock in one by one, carrying USB sticks containing the programs needed to operate the machines. "This can't be how things are being done," he said. After failing to find software that tied together the machines, workers, and processes on the factory floor, Caputo teamed up with Ellis in 2020 to build it themselves. Harmoni is now adding AI to its existing system. Its new product, HAL, uses the information Harmoni collects from its tablets to answer questions and take actions on the factory floor. Because the system already knows which machine is running, what job is underway, and what happened on previous runs, workers can ask HAL questions without first supplying that context. A worker could ask why a machine is running more slowly than expected, tell HAL to file a maintenance request, or flag the issue for the next operator. Caputo said that HAL allows workers to "literally speak to the machines." Harmoni installs a tablet on every machine in a factory. Harmoni WessDel, a San Jose manufacturer that makes precision components for aerospace and defense companies, has used Harmoni since 2024. Before Harmoni, workers had to line up at three different kiosks to clock in and manually enter information about their machines — tasks that Jeff McKay, WessDel's vice president, said could take nearly an hour of a worker's day. Now, workers can badge in by tapping their ID cards on Harmoni's tablets, which also automatically record machine activity. William Melek, a University of Waterloo engineering professor and director of its RoboHub, said tools like Harmoni's could help manufacturers cope with long-term labor shortages. A Deloitte and Manufacturing Institute study estimates US manufacturers could need 3.8 million additional workers by 2033, with about half of those jobs potentially going unfilled. Still, Melek said, technologies that automate parts of factory work could also draw pushback from unions concerned about their impact on jobs. Caputo said Harmoni is designed for factories that will continue to rely on people, with the goal of cutting repetitive administrative tasks rather than reducing head count. Many of Harmoni's customers, he added, already struggle to find enough workers. Some believe factory floors could eventually be staffed by humanoid robots . If that happens, Caputo said, Harmoni's system could coordinate them too. But he thinks that future is still a long way off. "The technology is just not there yet," he said. Have a tip? items.title: AI Models Are Watermarking Text—Will You Notice?
items.summary: On 11 August, Anthropic announced that all future Claude models will generate text that contains a watermark that identifies its results as AI generated. The company is not alone. Google has its own text watermark (which Anthropic’s is based on) it uses on the output of its Gemini models . OpenAI has yet to introduce a text watermark but it plans to do so . The rapid spread of watermarking is in part a response to the European Union’s AI Act , which mandates watermarks for AI models released after 2 August, 2026, along with other planned and proposed regulations aimed at curbing the spread of deceptive or manipulative AI-generated content. But the new rules may come at a cost for AI users who simply want the best possible results. AI watermarks can apply to many forms of content: The EU AI Act also requires them for images, audio, and video. Such media watermarks have been in use for years , and while their effectiveness as a holistic solution to marking AI remains up for debate , they can achieve detection rates above 99 percent . Image and video watermarks are already deployed by OpenAI, Google, and Meta, among others. (Anthropic doesn’t provide an image generation model.) Text watermarks have been less frequently deployed, however, and not everyone is convinced that text watermarking can work without compromising the quality of an AI model’s response. John Gruber, a prolific technology writer and co-creator of the Markdown language, calls the watermark a “ perversion of writing ” and disputes Anthropic’s assertion that a watermark doesn’t change the meaning or quality of text. Images consist of millions of pixels, he notes, whereas text responses often span just dozens or hundreds of words. Text seems to provide far less space to alter AI output in a way that is detectable yet not disruptive. John Kirchenbauer , postdoctoral fellow at the Vector Institute and co-author of a 2023 paper which was among the first to describe a text watermarking method, disagrees. “[A watermark] wouldn’t be detectable if there wasn’t a change. This is a very fundamental point,” he says. “The question is, do you care if it’s not the exact original distribution if, for all intents and purposes, it doesn’t change the utility to you?” Realistically, the issue comes down to that word, “utility.” Does watermarking AI-generated text meaningfully degrade the experience of the person using it? The answer is still under dispute. How AI Text Watermarks Work The term “watermark” is so familiar that it can cause confusion about how the technology works when applied to AI. Their skepticism stems from edge cases that can make a watermark more difficult to implement. On 11 August, Anthropic announced that all future Claude models will generate text that contains a watermark that identifies its results as AI generated. The company is not alone. Google has its own text watermark (which Anthropic’s is based on) it uses on the output of its Gemini models. OpenAI has yet to introduce a text watermark but it plans to do so.

The rapid spread of watermarking is in part a response to the European Union’s AI Act, which mandates watermarks for AI models released after 2 August, 2026, along with other planned and proposed regulations aimed at curbing the spread of deceptive or manipulative AI-generated content. But the new rules may come at a cost for AI users who simply want the best possible results.

AI watermarks can apply to many forms of content: The EU AI Act also requires them for images, audio, and video. Such media watermarks have been in use for years, and while their effectiveness as a holistic solution to marking AI remains up for debate, they can achieve detection rates above 99 percent. Image and video watermarks are already deployed by OpenAI, Google, and Meta, among others. (Anthropic doesn’t provide an image generation model.)

Text watermarks have been less frequently deployed, however, and not everyone is convinced that text watermarking can work without compromising the quality of an AI model’s response. John Gruber, a prolific technology writer and co-creator of the Markdown language, calls the watermark a “perversion of writing” and disputes Anthropic’s assertion that a watermark doesn’t change the meaning or quality of text. Images consist of millions of pixels, he notes, whereas text responses often span just dozens or hundreds of words. Text seems to provide far less space to alter AI output in a way that is detectable yet not disruptive.

John Kirchenbauer, postdoctoral fellow at the Vector Institute and co-author of a 2023 paper which was among the first to describe a text watermarking method, disagrees. “[A watermark] wouldn’t be detectable if there wasn’t a change. This is a very fundamental point,” he says. “The question is, do you care if it’s not the exact original distribution if, for all intents and purposes, it doesn’t change the utility to you?”

Realistically, the issue comes down to that word, “utility.” Does watermarking AI-generated text meaningfully degrade the experience of the person using it? The answer is still under dispute.

“If we sample from this modified distribution, then while any one token choice won’t necessarily come from that preferred set, over many samples, we’ll preferentially pick words from that up-weighted subset,” Kirchenbauer says.

The text watermark is embedded in the choice of words used, which is why it is effectively invisible to humans. Kirchenbauer and colleagues reported a detection rate of 98.4 percent, and zero false positives, in responses that contain about 200 tokens.
